settings.heading: The morning I counted the bottles.
settings.heading_em: And did the math I'd been avoiding.
settings.body:
I built Get Joy because of Cooper. That part of the story you may already know. What I haven't told as often is what happened after, once the food was solved and I thought the hard part was over.

It wasn't. Because the food handled the meals. It didn't handle everything else I'd been told Cooper needed on top of it.

A probiotic, because his gut needed support. A joint supplement, because the whole body was under stress. Fish oil, because every protocol mentioned inflammation. A digestive enzyme, because his stomach kept acting up between meals. A skin and coat supplement, because his coat had gone dull and I assumed it was separate from the food entirely.

Five different bottles. Five different schedules. Some you give with food, some you don't, some you have to remember twice a day.
settings.quote_text: I built the food to solve one problem. I didn't realize I'd just created five more.
settings.body_after: I was managing it like a part-time job. And I started wondering whether anyone else was doing the same thing, or whether I'd just made my life harder than it needed to be.

settings.heading: I had a counter full of bottles.
settings.heading_em: And most of them were trying to do one job.
settings.body:
I laid everything out one morning, actually laid it out, the way you do when something's bothering you and you can't say exactly what. Five bottles. Some half-empty. One I'd forgotten I'd bought twice.

Here's what each one actually cost me, and what I told myself it was for.
settings.col2_head: Why I told myself I needed it
settings.row1_why: His gut needs live bacteria. This was the starting point.
settings.row2_why: I kept reading that probiotics alone weren't enough.
settings.row3_why: Every protocol mentioned inflammation. This was supposed to help.
settings.row4_why: Apparently the bacteria need something to eat too.
settings.row5_why: His coat had gone dull. I assumed it was unrelated to the gut.
settings.offer_quote: One bag. See what changes in your dog. That's all I'm asking.

settings.body_after:
Around this time I called the same food scientist I'd worked with on the original formula. I described the stack, what I was buying, why I thought I still needed all of it. He asked me a question I hadn't actually thought through:

"Are any of these actually working together, or are they just sitting in the same dog?"

I didn't have a good answer. I'd been buying based on what each bottle claimed to do on its own. Nobody had ever asked whether a probiotic without the right prebiotic substrate even survives long enough to matter. Or whether the postbiotic layer, the part that actually does the work probiotics get credit for, was in any of these bottles at all.

It wasn't. Not in any of them.

settings.heading: I stopped buying pieces.
settings.heading_em: And started asking what a complete system actually looked like.
settings.body:
The honest answer was that I'd been buying ingredients, not a system. A probiotic supplement introduces bacteria. It doesn't feed them, and it doesn't do anything with what they produce once they're established. I was paying five times for one outcome that none of the five bottles were actually built to deliver together.

So I went back with a different question. Not "what else do I add," but "what would one chew look like if it carried the whole system instead of one piece of it."

The answer needed three things present at once, the same architecture we'd already built into the food, just now in something you could hand your dog in ten seconds instead of measuring into a bowl twice a day.

  • Probiotic. Bacillus coagulans and B. subtilis, spore-forming strains that survive stomach acid and arrive in the gut alive, where most strains die in the bottle or on the way down.
  • Postbiotic. 200mg, the layer almost nobody else includes. This is the part that does the work probiotics get credit for. Skip it, and you're paying for half a system.
  • Prebiotic. Inulin and kelp, food for the bacteria you just introduced. Without it, the colony you paid for doesn't hold.
  • L-Glutamine. 100mg, support for the gut lining itself, not just what's living on top of it.
  • Omega-3. Algae-sourced DHA and EPA, the same category I'd been buying as a separate bottle, now in the same chew.

We built it on the same Belly Biotics™ system that's already in the food. Same trademark, same logic, in something built for a different job: not a meal, a daily habit that doesn't require five separate ones next to it.

settings.heading: What I actually watched change.
settings.heading_em: And what I won't claim it did.
settings.body:
I'm careful with this part, because I've seen what happens when a company overpromises on a supplement, and I don't want to be that company.

What I'll tell you is what we measured. In a 60-day in-home study on daily probiotic supplementation with Belly Biotics™, the dogs in the study were 95% more likely to show improved health markers compared to the period before.
settings.stat_label: more likely to show improved health markers, in a 60-day in-home study on daily Belly Biotics™ supplementation.
settings.body_after:
I'm not telling you a chew fixes everything. I'm telling you what showed up when we measured it, and what I watched in my own routine once I stopped juggling five bottles and started giving one chew a day.

What customers typically notice, and when:
settings.step1_text: The chew goes in. No visible change yet. The strains are getting established.
settings.step2_text: Things start moving. Firmer, more regular stools are usually the first thing owners notice.
settings.step3_text: It settles in. Digestion steadies. Many owners mention fresher breath in this window.
settings.step4_text: The full picture. A more stable gut. This is why the routine is built around months, not days, same as it was with the food.

settings.heading: You're already doing more
settings.heading_em: than most dog owners ever will.
settings.body:
If you've read this far, you're the kind of owner who actually reads labels, who's already supplementing, who's already trying. That's not most people. Most people buy whatever's on the shelf at the pet store and move on.

You didn't. So I'm not going to pitch you on switching brands. I'm going to ask you to look at what you're currently giving your dog, the gut support, the omega, the joint or skin supplement if you have one, and add up what it's actually costing you. Not just in dollars. In bottles you have to remember, doses you have to track, refills you have to reorder on five different schedules.

That's the math I did at my own kitchen counter. It's the same math that led me to build this.

From Tom Arrix · Founder & CEO, Get Joy
